vignette:
Bounmy Phommasack is a 72-year-old Laotian-American man who works as a nanny for a family in the suburbs of Sacramento, California. He is married, soft-spoken, and widely regarded by the family he works for as gentle and unflappable - a man who has devoted his later years to the care of young children. What they do not know is that Bounmy arrives at work each morning carrying the weight of something that happened inside his own home, in a marriage that preceded his current one, decades ago and yet, in the most important sense, not over at all.

For several years during his fifties, Bounmy was in a relationship with a woman whose rages were unpredictable and, at their worst, physical. The assault that brought him to the present moment of seeking help occurred on an evening when the apartment was dark - she had turned the lights off before she came at him, and he had not seen her approach. She struck him repeatedly, and at one point pinned him against the kitchen wall, her hands at his throat. He did not fight back. He had never fought back. When it was over he slid to the floor in the dark and remained there for a long time, unable to tell whether the danger had passed.

In the years that followed, Bounmy rebuilt his life with considerable outward success. He remarried, found work he loved, and said very little about what had happened. But the event had left residue that did not dissolve with time. He had come to understand the darkness as something that carried threat inside it - not symbolically, but as a felt physical fact. In the Sacramento house where he works, the children sometimes run ahead of him and switch off hallway lights as a game, and in those moments Bounmy's body responds before his mind can intervene. His heart hammers. His shoulders pull inward. He finds himself pressing his back against the nearest wall, arms slightly raised, his body arranging itself into the exact posture he held on the kitchen floor that night - not as a choice but as something his muscles remember without being asked.

When the memory surfaces fully, it does not feel like his own history. He describes it with a kind of bewildered distance, as though he is recounting something that happened to a man he once read about. And yet the terror that accompanies it is entirely his own, immediate and total, as raw as it was the first time. These two qualities - the sense that the memory belongs to a stranger, and the feeling that the danger it contains is happening now - coexist in him without resolution.

Bounmy cannot relax. Even in his own living room, with his wife nearby and every light on, something in him remains at attention. An unexpected movement - a grandchild darting into his peripheral vision, a colleague stepping quickly around a corner at the family's house - produces a full-body startle, a sharp intake of breath, hands raised. He is embarrassed by this and works to conceal it. He has also made a quiet rule for himself: he will not be angry. Not ever, not even when anger would be reasonable. He had come to believe that anger in any form - his own or anyone else's - is the edge of something catastrophic, and so he smooths it away before it can form. He absorbs the frustrations of his work, the ordinary irritations of marriage, without reaction, and the effort of this costs him more than anyone around him can see.

Over the past year, Bounmy has quietly reorganised his life to avoid anything he experiences as stressful, which has meant declining social invitations, stepping back from a community group at his temple, and finding reasons not to attend the children's school events when they are held in the evening. His wife has noticed the withdrawal and named it, gently, more than once.

It was she who finally persuaded him to seek help. What Bounmy is most afraid of, sitting in a therapist's office for the first time at seventy-two, is that the terror he carries is simply who he is now. What he hopes, with a tentativeness he can barely articulate, is that someone might tell him otherwise.
